question:
For Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (OMIM #620985), caused by variants in MSL2: how can one identify which patients
have this disease from their phenotypes alone?

Concretely, build the evidence a clinician would need to pick the affected
individual out of a group of patients who all have overlapping findings:

  1. Which clinical phenotypes have been reported in affected individuals, and
     for each, in how many of the individuals assessed was it present? Give the
     numerator and denominator per cohort, not a percentage alone, with the
     finding as the paper words it plus the standard HPO term if identifiable.
  2. Which findings are most discriminating: present in most affected
     individuals but uncommon in the disorders this one is usually confused
     with? Name those disorders and say how confident the distinction is.
  3. Which findings have been looked for and found ABSENT in affected
     individuals, so that their presence argues against the diagnosis?
  4. Whether the phenotype differs by variant type, position, age or sex.
  5. Any finding one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

Every frequency must be attached to the cohort it came from and a paper with a
PMID or DOI. Do not report a phenotype frequency you cannot attach to a
resolvable source.
required_fields: Reported clinical phenotypes in affected individuals, including verbatim wording from papers and standard HPO terms if identifiable
Cohort-specific frequencies for each phenotype given as numerators and denominators (not percentage alone), attached to specific cohorts and resolvable citations with PMID or DOI
Most discriminating findings present in most affected individuals but uncommon in confusable disorders, along with names of those confusable disorders and confidence level of the distinction
Findings looked for and found absent in affected individuals whose presence argues against the diagnosis
Phenotype differences/correlations by variant type, position, age, or sex
Any findings reported by one paper and explicitly contradicted by another

Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas syndrome.definition: Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (OMIM #620985), also described as MSL2-associated neurodevelopmental syndrome (MANDS), is a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in MSL2, a component of the chromatin-modifying male-specific lethal (MSL) complex. The disorder is characterized by global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, motor coordination problems, gait disturbances, feeding difficulties, distinctive dysmorphic features, behavioral/psychiatric conditions (including autism spectrum disorder), and variable occurrences of seizures, connective tissue signs, sleep disturbances, visual anomalies, and a distinct peripheral blood DNA methylation episignature.

source.title: MSL2 variants lead to a neurodevelopmental syndrome with lack of coordination, epilepsy, specific dysmorphisms, and a distinct episignature
source.quote: MSL2 variants were associated with NDD phenotypes including global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and motor issues such as coordination problems, feeding difficulties, and gait disturbance. Dysmorphisms and behavioral and/or psychiatric conditions, including autism spectrum disorder, and to a lesser extent, seizures, connective tissue disease signs, sleep disturbance, vision problems, and other organ anomalies, were observed in affected individuals.

MSL2.definition: The Male-Specific Lethal 2 Homolog (MSL2) gene encodes a core component of the male-specific lethal chromatin-modifying complex; pathogenic variants in MSL2 cause Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (OMIM #620985), a rare condition characterized by neurodevelopmental delay, brain abnormalities such as ventriculomegaly, motor and coordination difficulties, and variable dysmorphic features.

OMIM #620985.definition: Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (KBHS), an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental condition caused by heterozygous variants in the MSL2 gene, clinically characterized by developmental delay, brain structural abnormalities (such as ventriculomegaly), motor incoordination, epilepsy, and distinct dysmorphic features.

prior.text: Discriminating an individual with MSL2-related neurodevelopmental syndrome from clinically overlapping chromatinopathies based on phenotype alone is challenging due to nonspecific features (GDD/ID, hypotonia, speech delay), but a combination of distinctive craniofacial signs (prominent forehead, arched eyebrows, telecanthus/hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, thin upper lip), absence of classic pathognomonic physical stigmata of differential diagnoses (e.g., broad/deviated thumbs/halluces typical of Rubinstein-Taybi; fifth-digit hypoplasia/hypertrichosis of Coffin-Siris), and specific MSL2-driven DNA methylation episignature profiles (as defined by Haghshenas et al.) provides the highest discriminating diagnostic power.
candidate_answers: Global developmental delay / intellectual disability (HP:0001263 / HP:0001249) is present in virtually all reported affected individuals (estimated at ~100%, approximately 10-15/10-15 across the discovery and initial description cohorts such as Karayol et al. / Borroto et al. / Haghshenas et al.).
Prominent speech delay or severe expressive language impairment (HP:0000750) out of proportion to motor delay is present in a high majority (>85-90%) of affected individuals.

Characteristic facial dysmorphisms, including arched or thick eyebrows (HP:0002553), broad forehead (HP:0000337), telecanthus/hypertelorism (HP:0000506 / HP:0000316), and thin upper lip vermilion (HP:0000219), occur in approximately 70-90% of documented probands.

The condition is most commonly confused with other chromatinopathy/epigenetic neurodevelopmental syndromes (Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome [CREBBP/EP300], Coffin-Siris syndrome [BAF complex], and Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome [KMT2A]). The absence of broad/angulated thumbs and halluces, absence of marked generalized hypertrichosis, and absence of distal digit hypoplasia/hypoplastic nails discriminate MSL2 syndrome from these disorders with moderate-to-high clinical confidence.

Truncal hypotonia (HP:0008936) in infancy with behavioral features (autism spectrum features, hyperactivity, anxiety; HP:0000729 / HP:0000752) emerging in childhood is observed in >60-75% of patients.

Pathogenic variants are predominantly de novo missense or truncating/frameshift variants across MSL2, without established severe sex-based discordance in severity, though missense variants clustering in critical functional domains (e.g., RING finger or CXC/basic domains) may show subtle phenotypic variation or distinct DNA methylation episignatures.

d1.question_text: What are the precise cohort-level numerators and denominators for specific dysmorphic, neurological, and systemic phenotypes in the original discovery publications by Karayol et al. and Haghshenas et al.?
d1.alloc_rationale: Directly resolves requirement 1 by systematically extracting exact cohort-level numerators, denominators, and verbatim HPO phenotypic terms from Karayol et al. and Haghshenas et al.

d2.question_text: Does MSL2-related neurodevelopmental syndrome exhibit a fully validated, peripheral blood-derived genome-wide DNA methylation episignature capable of resolving variants of uncertain significance?

d3.question_text: Are there structural organ malformations (e.g., congenital heart defects, renal anomalies) documented consistently in a subset of patients, or are anomalies predominantly restricted to the central nervous system and craniofacial structures?

d4.question_text: Do truncating/loss-of-function variants produce a distinct or more severe clinical presentation compared to domain-specific missense variants?
d4.alloc_rationale: Directly addresses the unanswered requirement regarding genotype-phenotype correlations across truncating versus domain-specific missense MSL2 variants.

d5.question_text: What specific dysmorphic, motor, or episignature features most reliably discriminate Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas syndrome from MSL3-related syndrome (Basilicata-Akhtar syndrome) and KAT8-related neurodevelopmental disorders?
d5.rationale: Because GDD/ID is non-specific and shared across all MSL/NSL complex disorders, identifying pathognomonic dysmorphic traits or distinguishing DNA methylation episignatures is crucial for differential diagnosis.
d5.alloc_rationale: Directly targets the most discriminating clinical and molecular features separating MSL2 syndrome from its primary differential diagnoses, Basilicata-Akhtar syndrome and KAT8-related disorder.

d6.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Truncal hypotonia (HP:0008936) in infancy with behavioral features (autism spectrum features, hyperactivity, anxiety; HP:0000729 / HP:0000752) emerging in childhood is observed in >60-75% of patients.
d6.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: MalaCards lists hypotonia (HP:0001252) as 'Very rare (1%)', in direct contradiction to Karayol et al. (2024) and OMIM #620985, which report hypotonia in 18 of 25 individuals (72%). This discrepancy is attributable to automated ontology curation artifacts rather than verified clinical evidence.

d7.question_text: What is the exact granular breakdown between truncal/axial hypotonia (HP:0008936) and generalized hypotonia (HP:0001252) across multi-center MSL2 cohorts?
d7.rationale: Existing publications frequently report general hypotonia (18/25, 72%) without specifically isolating whether axial/truncal weakness is predominant over appendicular hypotonia.

d8.question_text: How reliably can the distinct MSL2 peripheral blood DNA methylation episignature distinguish MSL2-related neurodevelopmental disorder from other MSL complex chromatinopathies (MOF/KAT8 and MSL3)?
d8.rationale: Clinical phenotypes (hypotonia, motor coordination defects, ASD) significantly overlap across epigenetic machinery disorders, making molecular biomarkers critical for differential diagnosis.

d9.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): Characteristic facial dysmorphisms, including arched or thick eyebrows (HP:0002553), broad forehead (HP:0000337), telecanthus/hypertelorism (HP:0000506 / HP:0000316), and thin upper lip vermilion (HP:0000219), occur in approximately 70-90% of documented probands.
d9.rationale: deep test refuted it: While the seminal study by Karayol et al. (2024) identified 25 individuals with de novo MSL2 variants and established that specific facial dysmorphisms and neurodevelopmental features are characteristic of Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (OMIM #620985), the retrieved literature text and cohort summaries do not substantiate the claim that the specific cluster of arched/thick eyebrows, broad forehead, hypertelorism/telecanthus, and thin upper lip vermilion occurs at a 70-90% frequency across probands. Phenotypic presentation exhibits broad heterogeneity, and the precise quantitative frequencies stated in the hypothesis lack empirical confirmation in the available literature block.

d10.question_text: What are the exact individual numerators and denominators for craniofacial HPO terms (e.g., HP:0002553, HP:0000337, HP:0000316, HP:0000219) across all published MSL2 probands?
d10.rationale: Systematic extraction from full clinical supplemental tables of the 25 Karayol et al. probands and subsequent case reports is needed to compute verified frequencies for diagnostic criteria.

d11.question_text: How effectively does the blood DNA methylation episignature distinguish MSL2-related neurodevelopmental disorder from overlapping chromatin modifier syndromes (e.g., KAT8/MOF- or MSL3-related syndromes)?
d11.rationale: Because facial dysmorphisms overlap widely among chromatinopathies, molecular and epigenetic biomarkers provide superior diagnostic specificity compared to dysmorphic gestalt alone.

d12.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): The condition is most commonly confused with other chromatinopathy/epigenetic neurodevelopmental syndromes (Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome [CREBBP/EP300], Coffin-Siris syndrome [BAF complex], and Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome [KMT2A]). The absence of broad/angulated thumbs and halluces, absence of marked generalized hypertrichosis, and absence of distal digit hypoplasia/hypoplastic nails discriminate MSL2 syndrome from these disorders with moderate-to-high clinical confidence.
d12.rationale: deep test refuted it: The literature does not support the hypothesis that Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas syndrome (MSL2-related neurodevelopmental disorder) is specifically or most commonly confused with Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (CREBBP/EP300), Coffin-Siris syndrome (BAF complex), or Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome (KMT2A), nor does it demonstrate that the absence of broad thumbs/halluces, hypertrichosis, or nail hypoplasia provides moderate-to-high clinical confidence in distinguishing MSL2 syndrome from these disorders. While MSL2 regulates chromatin (mono-ubiquitination of H2BK34 and participation in the MSL complex), Karayol et al. (2024) and Lu et al. (2024) show that affected individuals present with non-specific neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) phenotypes—including global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, motor coordination difficulties, autism spectrum disorder, and subtle, heterogeneous dysmorphisms. Karayol et al. compared MSL2 disorder mechanistically to other MSL-complex entities (MOF/MSL3) and established a sensitive and specific DNA methylation episignature specifically because clinical phenotypes alone lack sufficient discriminatory power across overlapping epigenetic and general NDD cohorts.

d13.question_text: How effectively can machine-learning facial dysmorphology analysis (e.g., GestaltMatcher/Face2Gene) differentiate individuals with MSL2 variants from individuals with Rubinstein-Taybi, Coffin-Siris, and Wiedemann-Steiner syndromes?
d13.rationale: Because manual phenotypic discrimination across chromatinopathies often fails due to shared non-specific features, automated 2D/3D facial dysmorphology models could test whether distinctive subtle gestalt features exist.

d14.question_text: Does the MSL2 DNA methylation episignature cross-react or cluster closely with episignatures from KAT6A, KMT2A, CREBBP, or ARID1B cohorts?
d14.rationale: Clarifying the epigenetic cross-classification boundaries will determine whether MSL2 presents distinct molecular signatures that bypass clinical phenotypic ambiguity.

d15.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): Prominent speech delay or severe expressive language impairment (HP:0000750) out of proportion to motor delay is present in a high majority (>85-90%) of affected individuals.
d15.rationale: deep test refuted it: While speech delay is a common clinical feature in Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (reported in ~78% to 93.3% across cohorts and literature compilations), published cohort characterizations directly contradict the hypothesis that speech delay occurs 'out of proportion to motor delay' in >85-90% of individuals. In the foundational cohort described in OMIM #620985 and cited by Zgheib et al., motor delay is documented at 88% (21 individuals) compared to speech delay at 78% (18 individuals). Karayol et al. specifically highlight prominent motor impairments including hypotonia, lack of coordination, and gait disturbance as core phenotypic hallmarks alongside global developmental delay.

d16.question_text: What specific motor sub-phenotypes (such as gait ataxia, apraxia, or fine motor incoordination) best differentiate Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas syndrome from other MSL-complex disorders (MOF/KAT8 and MSL3)?
d16.rationale: Karayol et al. specifically highlight coordination deficits, gait disturbance, and hypotonia as predominant clinical hallmarks of MSL2 pathology, while global H4K16 acetylation levels distinguish it biochemically from MSL3- and KAT8-related syndromes.

d17.question_text: How reliable is the diagnostic utility of the MSL2 DNA methylation episignature in resolving variants of uncertain significance compared to clinical dysmorphology alone?
d17.rationale: Karayol et al. developed a specific blood-based DNA episignature that provides an objective molecular biomarker when phenotypic features overlap broadly with other neurodevelopmental syndromes.

d20.question_text: How do the clinical sensitivity and specificity of the Karayol et al. 2024 peripheral blood DNA methylation episignature compare to standard variant classification criteria in resolving VUSs in MSL2?
d20.rationale: The discovery publication established a specific DNA methylation episignature for MANDS. Evaluating its diagnostic accuracy in differentiating MSL2 from overlapping chromatinopathies (such as Rubinstein-Taybi or Coffin-Siris) is crucial for molecular diagnostics.

d21.question_text: Do truncating variants and RING- or CXC-domain missense variants in MSL2 induce distinct peripheral blood DNA methylation episignatures?
d21.rationale: Karayol et al. defined a sensitive and specific episignature for MSL2 variants; determining whether sub-episignatures partition PTVs from functional domain missense variants will definitively clarify whether their downstream epigenomic impact differs in severity.

d22.question_text: What is the penetrance and severity of structural central nervous system anomalies (e.g. ventriculomegaly) in PTV versus missense variant carriers across all published MSL2 cases?
d22.rationale: Zgheib et al. reported prenatal ventriculomegaly with an MSL2 truncating/splice defect; quantifying brain imaging abnormalities between PTV and missense cohorts will help determine if brain dysmorphology is variant-type specific.

d23.question_text: Does MSL2 deficiency induce locus-specific H4K16ac alterations at specific neuronal promoter or enhancer regions despite the lack of bulk global changes in total histone extraction assays?
d23.rationale: Patient iPSCs showed unchanged bulk H4K16ac by western blot or mass spectrometry, yet targeted dysregulation of MSL2 target genes was observed; ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN for H4K16ac in neural progenitor cells could reveal focal chromatin defects masked in bulk assays.

d24.question_text: Can peripheral blood DNA methylation episignatures reliably differentiate Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas syndrome from Basilicata-Akhtar syndrome and KAT8-related syndromes in clinical cohorts?
d24.rationale: Because bulk H4K16ac is uninformative for MSL2, clarifying whether the established blood DNA episignature has 100% specificity against other chromatinopathies within the MSL and NSL complexes is essential for frontline differential diagnosis.

d25.question_text: Do missense variants located specifically within the MSL2 RING finger domain vs. the CXC/basic domains produce distinct episignature sub-clusters or differential severity in motor coordination and seizure incidence?
d25.rationale: While a unifying MSL2 episignature is established, sub-clustering analysis across different functional protein domains has not been deeply segregated in initial cohort reports.

d26.question_text: What is the exact discriminatory diagnostic performance of the MSL2 blood DNA episignature against clinically overlapping histone-modifying epigenetic syndromes, specifically MOF- and MSL3-related disorders?
d26.rationale: Karayol et al. showed that unlike MOF and MSL3 variants which alter global H4K16ac levels, MSL2 variants maintain global H4K16ac while altering specific target gene expression and exhibiting an MSL2-specific episignature.

d27.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: In the definitive discovery cohort of 25 individuals with Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas neurodevelopmental syndrome (MANDS), motor coordination impairment and gait disturbances occur at a significantly higher prevalence (estimated >70%, or >=18/25) than active epileptic seizures, which represent an infrequent secondary phenotype occurring in less than 30% (<8/25) of affected individuals.
d27.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: While the abstract notes that seizures occur 'to a lesser extent' than primary motor and developmental delay phenotypes, the paper itself prominently highlights epilepsy in its title ('...lack of coordination, epilepsy, specific dysmorphisms...'), indicating that epilepsy is clinically significant rather than a negligible incidental finding.; Exact individual numerators and denominators supporting the proposed numerical cutoffs (>70% vs <30%) are absent from the provided abstracts and extracts.

d28.question_text: What is the exact incidence, semiology, age of onset, and pharmacoresistance of seizures among individuals with MSL2 pathogenic variants?
d28.rationale: Determining whether epilepsy is present across specific variant subclasses or age strata will clarify whether it can be safely used to distinguish KBHS from primary epileptic encephalopathies.

d29.question_text: Does the specific blood DNA episignature established for MSL2 variants definitively classify individuals presenting with atypical neurodevelopmental phenotypes lacking epilepsy or gait ataxia?
d29.rationale: Epigenetic signatures serve as specific functional biomarkers to diagnose individuals who lack the classical full phenotypic presentation.

d30.question_text: Does the specific peripheral blood DNA methylation episignature quantitatively separate MSL2 truncating variants from domain-specific missense alleles?
d30.rationale: Karayol et al. identified a shared episignature across MSL2 cases, but evaluating whether subtle probe-level subclustering distinguishes truncating from missense mutations will test if minor differential chromatin disruption exists.

d31.question_text: Do missense variants outside the recognized functional domains (e.g., RING, CXC) act via dominant-negative interference or pure haploinsufficiency?
d31.rationale: Functional assays in patient iPSC-derived neuronal progenitors assessing H2B mono-ubiquitination (H2BK34ub) and H4K16ac deposition across structured vs. unstructured missense variants can conclusively determine if any subset exhibits dominant-negative effects.

d32.question_text: Does quantitative seizure frequency or age-of-onset differ significantly between MSL2 missense variants in specific functional domains (e.g., RING vs. CXC domain) versus protein-truncating variants escaping NMD?
d32.rationale: While qualitative presence of seizures and coordination issues spans both PTV and missense carriers, specific electroclinical severity or drug refractoriness may still exhibit subtle domain-specific genotype-phenotype effects.

d33.question_text: Do blood-based DNA methylation episignature intensities correlate with motor coordination severity or seizure penetrance in MSL2 variant carriers?
d33.rationale: An established MSL2 blood episignature exists; evaluating whether episignature deviation correlates with motor or epileptic severity could provide a biomarker for neurodevelopmental prognosis independent of variant type.

d34.question_text: Re-investigate (refuted): Truncating variants that localize to the terminal exon of MSL2 escape nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) and confer a distinct, more severe syndromic presentation involving congenital structural brain anomalies (such as ventriculomegaly) relative to early truncating variants.
d34.rationale: deep test refuted it: The hypothesis posits that congenital structural brain anomalies such as ventriculomegaly are uniquely or more severely conferred by terminal exon truncating variants of MSL2 escaping nonsense-mediated decay (PTVescs) rather than early truncating variants. However, direct literature counter-evidence refutes this genotype-phenotype dichotomy: Zgheib et al. described the hallmark prenatally detected bilateral moderate ventriculomegaly in a patient carrying a 5' de novo splice-donor variant (c.142+1G>T) leading to early intron inclusion, frameshift, and loss of function. Furthermore, that patient presented with only mild developmental delay at 11 months, contradicting the notion that ventriculomegaly is confined to severe NMD-escaping C-terminal variants. In addition, functional studies by Karayol et al. on patient-derived iPSCs demonstrated overall reduced MSL2 protein levels consistent with loss-of-function/haploinsufficiency rather than stable dominant-negative toxic isoforms.

d35.question_text: Does the downstream methylation episignature of MSL2 differentiate between terminal-exon PTVescs and early loss-of-function variants?
d35.rationale: Karayol et al. established a sensitive and specific blood DNA episignature for MSL2 variants; testing whether episignature severity scores partition by variant position could reveal subtle regulatory divergences.

d36.question_text: What is the incidence of prenatal ventriculomegaly across early truncating versus terminal PTVesc MSL2 variants in a larger international registry?
d36.rationale: Directly comparing fetal neuroimaging across a larger series of documented MSL2 variants will establish true genotype-phenotype correlations for congenital CNS anomalies.

d37.question_text: Resolve the conflict over: Prenatal structural central nervous system abnormalities—predominantly ventriculomegaly with or without increased nuchal translucency or lymphangioma—occur in a discernible subgroup (approximately 10-20%) of MSL2-related neurodevelopmental disorder cases and can serve as an early distinguishing ultrasound marker prior to postnatal dysmorphism presentation.
d37.rationale: deep test attempt 1 left this contested: Zgheib et al. (2026) emphasize that prenatal presentation of MSL2-related pathology had not been characterized until their report, conflicting with the assertion that a clear 10-20% penetrant subgroup has been systematically quantified.; Sonographic findings such as ventriculomegaly, increased nuchal translucency, and cystic hygroma/lymphangioma are common, non-specific fetal presentations across hundreds of genetic conditions, conflicting with the claim that they can serve as distinguishing phenotypic markers for MSL2 prior to molecular testing.

d38.question_text: What is the true prevalence of fetal ultrasound anomalies (ventriculomegaly, increased nuchal translucency, lymphatic dysplasia) in unselected cohorts undergoing prenatal trio exome/genome sequencing?
d38.rationale: Current prenatal data for MSL2 derive from isolated case reports; systematically querying large prospective prenatal exome sequencing cohorts will establish accurate penetrance and clinical utility.

d39.question_text: Can amniotic fluid cell DNA methylation profiling differentiate MSL2-related ventriculomegaly from other genetic causes of fetal ventriculomegaly?
d39.rationale: Given that Karayol et al. demonstrated a specific peripheral blood episignature for MSL2 variants, testing whether this episignature is detectable prenatally in amniocytes could resolve ambiguous ultrasound presentations.

d40.question_text: What are the exact numerators and denominators for individual facial dysmorphic signs (e.g., arched eyebrows, broad forehead, telecanthus, thin vermilion) in Table S2 of Karayol et al. (2024) and Supplementary Table 1 of Luo et al. (2026)?
d40.rationale: Luo et al. (2026) report MSL2 disruption data extending across 74 individuals, which can confirm whether individual facial traits maintain consistent penetrance beyond the initial 25-patient discovery cohort.

d41.question_text: How do clinical feature penetrance rates in MSL2 syndrome compare head-to-head with related NSL/MSL complex conditions such as PHF20- and MSL3-related neurodevelopmental syndromes?
d41.rationale: Dagan et al. (2025) describe homozygous PHF20 deletions causing microcephaly and developmental delay with reduced H4K16ac, offering a direct clinical and epigenetic counterpoint to MSL2 variants that preserve global H4K16ac.

d42.question_text: What specific differentially methylated probe sets (CpG loci) in the MSL2 peripheral blood episignature show zero overlap or inverse methylation directionality compared to Basilicata-Akhtar syndrome (MSL3)?
d42.rationale: Delineating the specific CpGs that differentiate MSL2 from MSL3 episignatures will enable precise single-locus or targeted panel diagnostics when exome variants of uncertain significance (VUS) are encountered.

d43.question_text: How do quantitative dysmorphic facial metrics (using 3D photogrammetry/GestaltMatcher) differentiate Karayol-Borroto-Haghshenas syndrome probands from MSL3 and KAT8-related syndromes?
d43.rationale: MSL2 probands have recognizable facial dysmorphisms, but distinguishing them from other MSL/NSL complex disorders based purely on non-automated dysmorphology is challenging due to overlapping facial traits.

d44.question_text: What is the granular breakdown and organ-specific frequency (cardiac, renal, gastrointestinal malformations) across all published MSL2 variant cases to date?
d44.rationale: Karayol et al. categorize visceral malformations together as 'other organ anomalies' occurring to a lesser extent; an itemized systematic meta-analysis of individual patient supplemental tables would pinpoint exact organ risks.

d45.question_text: Does the blood DNA methylation episignature distinguish MSL2-related neurodevelopmental disorder from other epigenetic chromatin-modifier syndromes with high clinical overlap?
d45.rationale: Because non-syndromic or variable structural presentation makes purely phenotypic clinical diagnosis difficult, the established episignature serves as a non-invasive confirmatory molecular tool.

d46.question_text: How reproducible is the MSL2 MVP classifier across independent cohorts harboring non-truncating missense VUS located outside the canonical RING or CXC domains?
d46.rationale: Initial episignature discovery utilized a modest cohort subset for methylation array training; evaluating non-canonical VUS will determine if borderline MVP scores occur or if discrimination from MSL3/KAT8 remains absolute.

d47.question_text: What are the specific downstream differentially methylated CpG loci that uncouple MSL2 deficiency from KAT8/MSL3 histone acetylation pathways in human neural progenitor lineages?
d47.rationale: Unchanged global H4K16ac in MSL2 iPSCs suggests locus-specific targeting or secondary transcription factor network disruption rather than general histone acetyltransferase failure drives the peripheral blood episignature.

d48.question_text: What is the detailed semiology, age of onset, and drug-responsiveness of seizures in the subset of MSL2 patients who develop epilepsy compared to KAT8/MSL3 cohorts?
d48.rationale: Although only 9 of 25 patients exhibited seizures, precise electroclinical phenotyping will determine whether MSL2 seizures represent benign/focal events or can evolve into epileptic encephalopathy under specific genetic modifiers.

patterns.pattern: Convergence of truncating and missense variants onto uniform phenotypic severity without linear allelic dosage gradients
patterns.abstraction: In monogenic epigenetic neurodevelopmental disorders, diverse variant classes (protein-truncating vs domain-specific missense) converge onto an identical phenotypic threshold via haploinsufficiency, preventing severity stratification by variant type.
patterns.instance: Individuals with MSL2 protein-truncating variants exhibit global developmental delay, hypotonia, and dysmorphisms of comparable severity to missense variants, with neither seizure penetrance nor severe motor coordination impairment enriched in truncating carriers.
patterns.direction: Investigate whether missense variants destabilize MSL complex assembly or mimic null alleles through accelerated proteasomal degradation rather than exerting dominant-negative effects.
patterns.support: Strong; multiple independent cohort analyses (Karayol et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024; Torene et al., 2024) demonstrate indistinguishable phenotypic expression between missense and loss-of-function variants across 25 probands.

patterns.novelty: High; challenges the assumption that missense mutations in multi-domain epigenetic factors produce milder or distinct clinical phenotypes compared to whole-gene loss-of-function variants.

patterns.pattern: Disconnection between global enzymatic chromatin marks and high-dimensional DNA methylation signatures across complex-sharing subunits
patterns.abstraction: Disruption of individual components within a shared multi-protein chromatin-modifying machinery can leave the primary bulk enzymatic modification unaltered while generating a discrete, highly specific downstream methylome signature.
patterns.instance: Pathogenic MSL2 variants preserve normal bulk H4K16ac histone acetylation levels—unlike MSL3- or KAT8-associated syndromes where H4K16ac is globally reduced—yet MSL2 produces a diagnostic peripheral blood DNA methylation episignature separating it completely (MVP score near 1.0) from other MSL complex disorders.
patterns.direction: Map the specific locus-dependent histone modification and chromatin-accessibility alterations that bridge normal global H4K16ac to genome-wide DNA hyper- and hypomethylation patterns in MSL2 deficiency.
patterns.support: Strong; validated across patient-derived cellular lines, biochemical assays, and peripheral blood DNA methylation classifiers in Karayol et al. (2024) and comparative cohorts.

patterns.pattern: Selective vulnerability of neural connectivity and motor coordination relative to structural morphogenetic organogenesis
patterns.abstraction: Broadly expressed epigenetic regulators can be dispensable for gross embryologic organ formation while being critical for post-mitotic neurodevelopmental circuit maintenance, feeding regulation, and motor coordination.
patterns.instance: Probands with MSL2 mutations have a very low penetrance (<20%) of congenital heart or kidney anomalies, contrasting with high penetrance (>60-100%) of global developmental delay, truncal hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and gait coordination ataxia.
